title: SQL
lead: Relational terminology, single-table queries, aggregation, joins and nested queries.
goals: Queries over multiple tables and joins

sections.title: Relational terminology and single-table queries
sections.html:
SQL history and declarative execution

SQL originated in IBM’s System R work in the 1970s, was commercialised by relational DBMSs and standardised by ANSI/ISO. The source references SQL:2023. Different engines implement different subsets and extensions.

SQL specifies result conditions, not a particular search or join algorithm. That allows the DBMS to replace the physical plan while preserving rows, multiplicities and other specified semantics. This lecture covers relational terminology, single-table queries, aggregates, joins and subqueries.

PDF pp. 1–5

Schema, bag instances and the source database

A relation schema fixes attribute names and types. A tuple is one record; an attribute is one column. SQL instances are bags, so repeated rows are meaningful unless a constraint or DISTINCT removes them. DDL defines structures, DML accesses/modifies data and DCL controls privileges.

The source Student and Enrolled rows used for the first queries are shown below. Course additionally stores cid, name and year. Later ORDER BY and OUTER JOIN slides use separate demonstration rows; their figures must not be treated as results of this initial instance.

Student(sid, name, dept, age)
12344  Jones  CS       18
12355  Smith  Physics  23
12366  Gold   CS       21
Enrolled(sid, cid, grade)
12344  INF-10080  65
12355  INF-11199  72
12355  INF-11122  61
12366  INF-10080  80
12344  INF-11199  53

PDF pp. 6–9

SELECT, DISTINCT, ordering and limits

SELECT * FROM Student WHERE age = 18 returns Jones’s row in the initial instance. SELECT lists columns or expressions. DISTINCT compares the complete projected row, not just its first attribute.

ORDER BY grade DESC, sid ASC first sorts by descending grade, then breaks equal-grade ties by increasing sid. In the ordering slide, (12311,76) precedes (12355,72), then (12399,72), then (12344,53). LIMIT 3 keeps the first three of the chosen order; OFFSET 1 skips its first row. A deterministic top-k requires a specified order, including tie-breakers when needed.

PDF pp. 10–12

sections.title: Aggregation, GROUP BY and HAVING
sections.html:
Aggregate state and grouping rules

COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarise input values. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) excludes NULL values. GROUP BY dept creates one group per department value, and AVG(age) is computed separately in each group.

SELECT dept, name, AVG(age) ... GROUP BY dept is invalid in the form taught unless name is also grouped or a supported functional-dependency rule determines it. Otherwise several names compete for one group output. Adding name to GROUP BY changes the groups; it is not merely a syntax repair preserving the original question.

PDF pp. 13–15

HAVING and logical evaluation

SELECT dept, AVG(age) AS avg_age
FROM Student
GROUP BY dept
HAVING AVG(age) > 21;

WHERE filters original rows; it cannot generally filter on an aggregate alias that has not been computed. HAVING filters completed groups. Using the source’s separate group-result figures CS=20.5, Physics=21.1 and Maths=19.8 leaves Physics. Those illustrative aggregates are not recalculations of the earlier three Student rows.

Logical order is FROM → WHERE → grouping/aggregates → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Physical execution may reorder work only when results remain equivalent.

PDF pp. 16–18

sections.title: Queries over multiple tables and joins
sections.html:
Join query and equivalent forms

SELECT S.name, E.grade
FROM Student AS S JOIN Enrolled AS E ON S.sid = E.sid
WHERE E.cid = 'INF-11199';

On the initial source data, the result rows are (Smith,72) and (Jones,53), without a promised order. The comma-FROM form with equality in WHERE expresses the same inner join. The conceptual Cartesian product need not be materialised: the engine can filter Enrolled first and use a join algorithm.

NATURAL JOIN equates all shared attribute names. It is equivalent here because sid is the intended shared name; adding another same-named attribute can change its meaning.

PDF pp. 19–22

All outer-join result rows

These slides change the instance: Student has 121/Jones, 122/Smith, 123/Gold; Enrolled has (121,65), (123,72), (121,61), (201,53) after suppressing cid. Matched name/grade pairs are Jones/65, Jones/61 and Gold/72.

LEFT adds Smith/NULL. RIGHT instead adds NULL/53. FULL includes both additional rows. One Jones row yields two outputs because two enrolments match. NULL padding applies only to the missing side, and unmatched rows are identified by the ON condition before later WHERE filtering.

PDF pp. 23–25

sections.title: Nested queries and set comparisons
sections.html:
Nested, correlated and quantified queries

SELECT S.name FROM Student AS S
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM Enrolled AS E
  WHERE E.sid = S.sid AND E.cid = 'INF-11199'
);

IN over the matching Enrolled student IDs answers the same enrolment question. EXISTS asks only whether a witness exists, so SELECT 1 is sufficient. Correlation means the condition uses the current outer S.sid; an optimiser may decorrelate it rather than literally rerun a full scan for each row.

ANY needs at least one true comparison; ALL needs all comparisons true, subject to SQL’s UNKNOWN rules. IN is = ANY; NOT IN is <> ALL. EXISTS depends on rows, not whether their selected values are NULL. NOT IN can become UNKNOWN if no equal value is found but NULL is present. For an empty subquery, ANY/EXISTS are false and ALL/NOT EXISTS true.

PDF pp. 26–29

quiz.question: In Sale, what is Hue’s total after WHERE amount >= 30?
quiz.explanation: The row with amount=10 is filtered out, leaving 30+90=120. WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY computes SUM, so the sale of 10 does not contribute.
